title: The contented served
hookLine: those who served in contentment and meditated on truth were accepted (Asa di Var, ang 466)

cards: Visit a big gurdwara kitchen early in the morning. Someone is stirring a pot of dal the size of a bathtub. Someone is rolling rotis at a speed that looks impossible.
An old man is stacking steel plates. Nobody is checking a clock, and nobody is waiting for thanks. Ask one of them why they're there, and they might just shrug and hand you a ball of dough.
Guru Nanak described people like this in a single pauri, and it turns on one word.

teach.b: The pauri is on ang 466, and it opens like this, in paraphrase: those who served were the contented ones, the ones who meditated on truth and nothing but truth. The word is santokh. Contentment.
You've met it before on this path: Japji calls contentment one of the earrings of the true yogi. Here, it's what makes service real. Then the pauri describes these people.
They did not set their foot on the path of wrong. They did good and lived by dharam, by righteousness.

teach.h: THEY DID GOOD AND ATE LITTLE.
teach.b: They broke the world's chains, and they ate and drank only a little. Then it turns to the One: you are the great giver, always giving more. By greatness, the Great One is found.
So why contentment, of all things?
Think about what discontent does to service. Serve hoping to be noticed, and every unnoticed hour stings. Serve to get something back, and you're keeping score.
Serve while wishing you were somewhere else, and the work feels heavy, and so do you. Contentment takes all of that out. It doesn't mean wanting nothing for the world.
It means being at peace with your own share while you work for others. Eating a little is part of the picture: not needing much leaves room for giving.
In Sikh life, seva, selfless service, is everywhere: in the langar, in cleaning shoes, in sweeping the floor. This pauri gives seva its inner side.
The hands serve. The heart is content.
And the pauri says the ones who served that way were accepted.

how: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara kitchen, cleaning, and serving the community, and this pauri of Asa di Var describes the contented spirit behind it.

o: having too little left to give
contentment, at peace with your share
a calm that comes from praise

games.q: the contented servants — tap the pairs.
p: the great giver, always giving more

s: in this pauri, contentment means wanting nothing for anyone
it means peace with your own share while working for others.
the pauri says the contented ones meditated on truth
they served and dwelt on truth, nothing but truth.
the pauri praises those who ate and drank little
not needing much leaves room for giving.

games.q: you've been serving in the langar for hours and nobody has thanked you. what does the pauri's servant do?
o: keep serving, content, without keeping score.
tell people how long you've been there.
games.why: the pauri's servants were the contented ones. their service was accepted because the heart wasn't keeping score.

practice: Pick one small service you could do soon, washing a few dishes, refilling someone's water, and breathe out any wish to be noticed.
Picture yourself doing it fully, finishing, and walking away without needing anyone to see, and feel what that's like in your chest. If you pray, say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Santokh, contentment: Guru Nanak's picture of true servants, content with little through santokh, rooted in truth, doing good without keeping score.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: santokh, contentment; one of the virtues Gurbani returns to again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: contented service. The hands serve; the heart is at peace. That's day five hundred forty-five.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, pauri 7 (sev keetee santokhee-een), Ang 466
